newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Iranian Red Crescent set to end rescue operations.
newsitem.headline: Iranian Red Crescent set to end rescue operations.

text.p: The Iranian Red Crescent reached two isolated mountain villages struck by the earthquake -- thought to be the last searched -- and may end rescue operations at nightfall, a world disaster relief body said on Tuesday.
Pledges have come in "thick and fast" in response to an appeal to help victims of the huge quake, the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies also said.

"The last two villages have been searched by Iranian Red Crescent rescue workers," Marie-Francoise Borel, Federation spokeswoman in Geneva, told Reuters after receiving the latest report from its member, the Iranian Red Crescent Society.
"Rescue operations may end tonight, but it is not confirmed," she added.
The spokeswoman for the Federation, which groups 171 national Red Cross and Red Crescent member societies, welcomed news that Iran had lowered its numbers for casualties of Saturday's massive quake.

A senior Interior Ministry official in Qaen, near the epicentre in the eastern region, said 1,560 people had been killed and 2,810 injured. No explanation was given for previous official reports that about 2,400 had died and 6,000 were injured.
"We are very pleased if the tragic numbers are down," Borel said. "It had been difficult to get exact numbers."

The Iranian Red Crescent on Tuesday also reported 1,560 dead and 4,463 injured, echoing the new death toll but giving a higher number of casualties than the Interior Ministry official, according to the figures provided to the Federation.
It was not known if any new victims were identified in the two "small and remote" mountain villages reached on Tuesday.
"Shelter items are the priority now. Tents and blankets are needed, as well as water tanks," the spokeswoman said.
Between Monday and Tuesday, the Federation raised 7.5 million Swiss francs ($five million) toward its 12 million swiss franc ($8.2 million) appeal issued for Iran on Monday.

The money was raised from four governments -- Britain, Denmark, Netherlands and Norway -- and from 15 national Red Cross or Red Crescent societies in Algeria, Austria, Belgium, Britain, Canada, Denmark, the Netherlands, Germany, Kuwait, Japan, Libya, Norway, Sweden, Switzerland and Turkey. The EU's humanitarian agency ECHO also contributed.
But 4.5 million swiss francs ($three million) more is badly needed in Iran, where 60,000 to 65,000 were left homeless and many villages lack clean drinking water, the Federation said.

"The pledges have been coming in thick and fast all day -- we are struggling to remember when there has been such a rapid and generous reaction over a 24-hour period to an appeal for a natural disaster," said Margareta Wahlstroem, under-secretary general for disaster response, said in an overnight statement.

The funds are being used to provide vital relief supplies -- including emergency food, shelter, clothing, cooking utensils water and hygiene items -- for at least 60,000 people over the next four months.
Relief goods have been flown into the airport at Meshat, north of the affected zone, according to Borel. They are then being taken by truck or helicopter to the area for distribution.
The Iranian Red Crescent has been working around the clock, deploying 4,300 rescue workers within hours of the quake.
"It has distributed all emergency food stocks and relief items. Its warehouses are now empty," the Federation said.
Meanwhile United Nations agencies have pledged $360,000 to Iran's victims, the world body announced in New York on Monday.

The U.N. Department of Humanitarian Affairs (DHA), which has provided an emergency grant of $50,000 to purchase relief supplies locally, sent a two-member team to Iran on Tuesday to carry out disaster assessment and coordinate efforts.
Plastic water containers, cookers, lamps, power generators, shoes and clothing, canned food, blankets and medicine were needed on an emergency basis, according to the DHA statement.
